Chapter 8: The Emotional Rewards of Reclaiming the Kitchen
If you’ve ever dreaded stepping into the kitchen, you’re definitely not alone. It’s so easy to miss the quiet joys that can come from just feeding yourself. But what if making a meal—even something really simple—could be a small act of care? A way to grab a little control when life feels overwhelming?
Picture this: a college student, far from home, feeling that ache of homesickness and disconnection. One night, she decides to cook the simplest version of her mother’s soup—just broth, noodles, and a few veggies. As the pot simmers, the kitchen fills with that familiar scent, and suddenly, she feels just a little less alone. The meal’s not perfect, but it’s comforting. And in that moment, she realizes—she can take care of herself, even in these small ways.
Most of us don’t notice just how much power there is in these everyday rituals. The author shares stories of people who, after years of avoiding the kitchen, find real satisfaction in making their own meals. There’s something special about turning a handful of ingredients into something that nourishes you. Even cleaning up afterwards can feel grounding—a simple way to close out the day and bring a little order to your space.
Cooking can also pull us closer to others. Imagine a group of friends, all with totally different schedules and tastes, starting a tradition of “potluck nights.” Each person brings something simple—store-bought or homemade, it doesn’t matter. Sharing food like this, no matter how humble, becomes a real source of comfort and community.
So, the kitchen doesn’t have to be a place of stress or failure. With a bit of practice—and a lot of self-compassion—it can grow into a space for small victories, quiet moments, and even joy. Maybe the emotional rewards aren’t obvious at first, but over time, they really add up—building confidence, resilience, and that deep sense of belonging we all crave.
